Recovery should ride the existing accumulator recovery ("slowly recovered") — the wake stays smooth for many short-wave periods, i.e. seconds, which the `min(J, recover)` accumulator already encodes. This gives the streak-film tonal layer a physically correct optical behavior at near-zero cost and zero feedback risk: derivative attenuation at shade time never enters the compute-pass Jacobian.

### Stability: the loop is real, and three cheap ways to break it

The oscillation concern is real as a mechanism: damping the small cascade's horizontal displacement raises `J` toward 1 (fewer folds) -> less foam injection -> the accumulator decays -> damping releases -> `J` drops -> foam re-injects — a relaxation oscillator with period approximately equal to the accumulator recovery time. No published post-mortem of this failure exists (nothing shipped couples the loop at all), but the analogous problem is solved in operational wave models: [WAM / WAVEWATCH III](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/263108814_Validation_of_whitecap_fraction_and_breaking_wave_parameters_from_WAVEWATCH-III_using_in_situ_and_remote-sensing_data) apply a whitecapping dissipation source term `S_ds` as part of the source balance and must integrate it *semi-implicitly* because dissipation feedback is stiff — the oceanographic precedent that naive explicit feedback on the dissipation term is unstable and that implicit or lagged treatment fixes it. Three structural fixes, in order of robustness:

1. **One-way coupling.** Compute `J` and the accumulator in the compute pass from the *undamped* displacement/derivative maps (poseidon already does: the accumulator pass reads raw FFT outputs), and apply attenuation only downstream where the surface is assembled and shaded. The foam-generation signal then never sees the damping; the loop is open by construction. The only "inconsistency" — foam born from folds slightly sharper than rendered — is invisible, since the fresh cap covers exactly those texels with opaque foam.
2. **Vertical-only crumble displacement.** `J` contains only horizontal-displacement gradients (Tessendorf eq. 44–45), so a vertical bump cannot feed back even under two-way coupling.
3. **Hysteresis, if two-way coupling is ever wanted** (e.g. damped `J` for the strain/carve signal): drive damping from a slower low-passed copy of the accumulator (fast attack, slow release — a second recover constant), and clamp attenuation to ≤ ~0.5 so damped `J` cannot cross back over the foam threshold `M`.

Auxiliary evidence that runtime displacement composition per se is stable and shipped: [Crest's dynamic-wave sim](https://crest.readthedocs.io/en/4.14/user/ocean-simulation.html) adds interactive displacement onto FFT waves ("damping controls how much energy is dissipated each frame and helps sim stability"); [Atlas (GDC 2019, Mihelich & Tcheblokov)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Dqld965-Vv0) composes wake and explosion displacement with the WaveWorks sea; and War Thunder's distance-driven cascade fade is spatial attenuation of the identical kind.

For poseidon: the architecture is already one-way-safe — the turbulence accumulator lives in a compute pass fed by raw displacement derivatives, and foam is fragment-only — so accumulator-weighted attenuation of the 24 m cascade applied in the vertex/fragment surface assembly *cannot* oscillate; the compute-side `J` never sees it. The one rule to enforce: never sample the damped maps back into the accumulator update or into the strain (divergence) signal that sets carve thresholds; if strain is wanted from damped fields for visual consistency, use the low-passed accumulator copy (fix 3). Suggested starting point: `attenuation = 1 - a*smoothstep(t0, t1, trailAccumulator)`, with `a <= 0.5` for displacement and `a <= 0.85` for the cascade's normal-derivative contribution.

### How much crest softening is actually visible: the energy budget

[Rapp & Melville 1990](https://royalsocietypublishing.org/doi/10.1098/rsta.1990.0098) ("Laboratory measurements of deep-water breaking waves", Phil. Trans. R. Soc. A 331 — the standard reference): a single breaking event removes ~10% (spilling) to ~25% (plunging) of the wave packet's excess energy and momentum flux, with >90% of that loss dissipated within *four* wave periods. Since height ∝ √energy, the crest that just broke is only ~5% (spilling) to ~13% (plunging) lower afterward — the profile-height change alone is a second-order visual cue. [Iafrati 2011](https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1029/2011JC007038) (JGR Oceans) confirms the spilling ~10% figure numerically. The stronger cue is kinematic: crests slow dramatically at breaking — [Banner et al. 2014](https://journals.aps.org/prl/abstract/10.1103/PhysRevLett.112.114502) (PRL 112:114502) measured a systematic ~20% crest-speed slowdown at breaking onset (crests advance at ~0.8x the linear phase speed; spilling whitecap fronts average ~0.87x per laboratory packet measurements; Barthelemy et al.'s breaking-onset criterion is particle speed ≈ 0.84–0.85x crest speed — see also [Fedele et al., JFM](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/journal-of-fluid-mechanics/article/crest-speeds-of-unsteady-surface-water-waves/BA1C8F5D38A049FED4A99323235D2B30)). The wave that broke is left with a *rounded*, decelerated crest riding a visibly smoothed wake (Ermakov's suppression), while the sharp specular profile persists only on unbroken neighbors. The net ranking of what reference footage actually shows at 100 m+ viewing distance: (1) foam brightness/pattern — dominant; (2) the smooth dark/glossy wake scar where short waves are suppressed — strong in glinty light; (3) whitecap fronts lagging the wave field at ~0.8c; (4) crest profile rounding — resolvable mainly within roughly the footprint of the smallest cascade's waves, i.e. close-ups where individual crest silhouettes subtend many pixels.

For poseidon: decision guidance. A 5–13% height reduction on a breaking crest of the 144 m cascade is under a pixel at most framings — full displacement feedback on the mid cascade is not worth its cost or risk. What the footage supports, in cost order: (1) normals-domain suppression of the 24 m cascade plus glint kill in the trail band — biggest visible payoff, zero risk; (2) a fresh-cap-band treatment of the 24 m cascade's *displacement* (one-way, ≤50%) so whitecapped crests lose their sharpest sub-structure for close and rail framings — matched to the 4-wave-period dissipation timescale, i.e. attack over ~1–2 s for the small cascade's sub-second waves, release with the accumulator; (3) a vertical-only crumble bump (accumulator-gated fbm, amplitude scaled to a fraction of the 24 m cascade's amplitude, advected with the existing 0.35x flow-warp coordinates) — provably feedback-free, only worth it for close framings; (4) the crest-speed lag (~0.8c) is unreproducible without restructuring and is the cue to consciously forgo. Skip mid-cascade displacement feedback entirely. The 10–25% energy numbers also calibrate any damping magnitude: total local attenuation of the small cascade beyond ~25% of *energy* (≈13% of amplitude) in the fresh band exceeds what a single real breaking event removes from the wave train as a whole — though the small-wavelength band locally loses far more (Ermakov's 3–10x), which is why the split treatment — mild displacement damp, strong derivative damp — is the physically literate combination.
